question: What should I look for in a fractional CRO in Indiana?
body:
## Direct Answer

When hiring a fractional CRO in Indiana, look for a proven revenue leader who has scaled companies of your size and stage, understands the Midwest B2B buyer and Indiana's manufacturing, logistics, insurance, and life-sciences economy, and will commit enough weekly hours to actually own the number rather than merely advise. The best candidates bring a documented playbook, references from similar-stage founders, comfort with your existing tech stack, and a clear 90-day plan tied to pipeline and net revenue retention — not a vague promise of "strategy." Prioritize outcome accountability, cultural fit with a lean team, and a fee structure that aligns their upside with yours.

A fractional Chief Revenue Officer is a part-time, senior revenue executive who takes real ownership of sales, marketing, and customer success alignment for a fraction of a full-time CRO's cost. For Indiana companies — often bootstrapped or lightly funded manufacturers, SaaS startups in the Indianapolis tech corridor, or services firms in Fort Wayne, Bloomington, and Evansville — this model delivers senior firepower without a $350K+ salary and equity grant. But the market is noisy: plenty of self-styled "fractional CROs" are really lead-gen consultants or LinkedIn coaches. The screening criteria below separate operators who move the number from advisors who produce slide decks.

## What does a fractional CRO actually own versus a consultant

The single most important distinction is ownership. A true fractional CRO carries the revenue number. They set the plan, hire and coach the reps, sit in on deals, own the forecast, and answer for the result in your board or leadership meeting. A consultant, by contrast, diagnoses and recommends — the accountability boomerangs back to you. When you interview candidates in Indiana or anywhere else, ask directly: "Will you own the pipeline number, or advise me on it?" The answer reveals which category they belong to, and it should be reflected in how their engagement is structured and compensated.

Ownership shows up in the details of the engagement. A real CRO wants access to your CRM, wants to run the weekly pipeline review, wants to be in the room for QBRs, and wants a variable component tied to bookings or net revenue retention. Someone selling you a fixed monthly retainer with no performance tie and a two-day-a-month cadence is a consultant with a fancier title. Neither is wrong for every situation — early-stage founders sometimes just need advisory pattern-matching — but you must know which one you're buying. For a deeper breakdown of the role's scope, see the [fractional CRO responsibilities guide](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/q11201).

The following diagram maps the decision between the two engagement types based on what your company actually needs right now.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Revenue problem identified] --> B{Do you need someone to own the number}
    B -->|Yes| C[Fractional CRO with variable pay]
    B -->|No just guidance| D[Advisory consultant on retainer]
    C --> E{Team exists to lead}
    E -->|Yes| F[CRO coaches and runs cadence]
    E -->|No| G[CRO hires builds and runs cadence]
    D --> H[Diagnostic and recommendations]
    F --> I[Accountable for pipeline and NRR]
    G --> I
    H --> J[You stay accountable]
```

## Why does Indiana market knowledge matter for a fractional CRO

Indiana's economy is not Silicon Valley's, and a revenue leader who has only ever sold venture-backed SaaS to coastal buyers may misread the room here. The state's revenue base leans heavily on advanced manufacturing, logistics and distribution (Indianapolis is a national freight hub), insurance and financial services, agribusiness, and a fast-growing life-sciences and med-tech cluster anchored by companies like Eli Lilly, Roche Diagnostics, and Cook Medical. Buyers in these sectors tend to be relationship-driven, value long-cycle trust over aggressive closing tactics, and expect a vendor who understands operational realities on the plant floor or in the clinic. A CRO who tries to run a hyper-scaled, high-velocity inside-sales motion against a procurement-heavy manufacturing buyer will stall.

There is also a talent and cost dimension. Sales compensation, cost of living, and the available rep talent pool in Indiana differ meaningfully from the coasts, which changes how you build and budget a team. A fractional CRO who knows the local market can tell you what a strong enterprise AE actually costs in Indianapolis versus Chicago, where to recruit from (Purdue, Indiana University, Butler, and the growing 16 Tech and Elevate Ventures ecosystems produce strong go-to-market talent), and how to structure quotas that are competitive without overpaying. This local calibration is one of the highest-leverage things a regionally fluent CRO brings, and it is invisible on a generic national résumé.

That said, do not over-index on "Indiana experience" to the exclusion of stage and motion fit. A CRO who scaled a Cincinnati or Columbus B2B company from $3M to $15M ARR and understands Midwest buyers is often a better fit than someone who happens to live in Carmel but has only run enterprise deals at a Fortune 500. Weigh regional fluency as one important factor among several, alongside the stage-and-motion match covered in the [revenue leader hiring criteria](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/q11207).

## How do you evaluate a fractional CRO's track record

Track record is where most hiring mistakes happen, because impressive-sounding titles hide wildly different realities. The question is not "Were you a CRO?" but "What did the number do while you owned it, at a company like mine, and what specifically did you do to move it?" Push for concrete, verifiable outcomes: starting and ending ARR, the time window, the motion (inbound, outbound, channel, product-led), the team size they inherited versus built, and the specific levers they pulled. Vague claims like "grew revenue 300%" are meaningless without the base, the timeframe, and their actual contribution versus market tailwinds.

Stage fit is critical. Scaling a company from $1M to $5M is a fundamentally different job than taking one from $20M to $50M — the first is about finding and repeating a motion, the second about operationalizing and layering management. A CRO whose entire career was spent at post-Series-C companies with big budgets and established brands may be lost in a scrappy, capital-efficient Indiana environment where every dollar is scrutinized. Conversely, a pure early-stage builder may not have the process rigor a $30M company needs. Match the candidate's proven zone to where you actually are.

References are non-negotiable, and you should insist on speaking to founders or CEOs the candidate reported to, not just peers or reports who might be friendly. Ask those references pointed questions: Would you hire them again? Did they own the number or make excuses? How did they handle a quarter that missed? Were they a culture-add or a culture-drain on a lean team? The best signal is a former client who is willing to say, unprompted, "Call me anytime — they saved us." For a structured reference-check framework, the [revenue leadership due diligence checklist](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/q11215) walks through the exact questions to ask.

## What tech stack and RevOps fluency should they have

A modern fractional CRO must be fluent in the systems that run revenue, because in a lean Indiana company they will not have a large RevOps team to lean on — they may be the RevOps function for the first several months. At minimum, expect deep comfort with a CRM (HubSpot dominates the mid-market and startup segment; Salesforce shows up in larger and more complex organizations), forecasting discipline, and the reporting rigor to produce a pipeline number leadership can trust. If a candidate cannot speak fluently about pipeline stages, conversion rates by stage, sales cycle length, and CAC payback, they are not operating at the CRO altitude.

The right level of tooling fluency depends on your maturity. A pre-revenue or early company needs a CRO who can stand up a clean, simple CRM and a repeatable process from scratch without over-engineering — the classic failure mode is a leader who insists on enterprise tooling a five-person team cannot sustain. A $15M+ company needs someone who can rationalize an already-messy stack, unify sales, marketing, and customer success data, and build the reporting spine that supports forecasting and board reporting. Ask candidates to describe the last revenue tech decision they made and, crucially, one they chose *not* to make because it was premature. The restraint answer is often more telling than the build answer.

The diagram below shows the core RevOps functions a fractional CRO should be able to align, regardless of your stage.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[Fractional CRO] --> B[Sales]
    A --> C[Marketing]
    A --> D[Customer Success]
    B --> E[Pipeline and forecast]
    C --> E
    D --> E
    E --> F[One revenue number]
    F --> G[Board and leadership trust]
```

Fluency also means knowing what to measure and what to ignore. A strong CRO focuses the team on a small set of leading indicators — qualified pipeline created, stage conversion, cycle time, and net revenue retention — rather than drowning everyone in vanity dashboards. If a candidate's first instinct is to propose fifteen new reports, that is a yellow flag. The goal is clarity and action, not analytics theater. See the [RevOps metrics that matter guide](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/q11220) for the short list a CRO should anchor on.

## How should you structure hours, fees, and the engagement

The economics of a fractional engagement determine whether you get an owner or a tourist. Most legitimate fractional CROs commit somewhere between one and three days a week — roughly 8 to 24 hours — and charge either a monthly retainer or a day rate, often with a performance component. National ranges vary widely, so rather than anchor on a specific number, focus on the ratio of commitment to price: a CRO billing for two days a week but only reachable for two hours is overcharging, and one promising to own a full sales team on four hours a month is overpromising. Get the weekly hour commitment in writing, and tie it to specific deliverables and cadences.

Alignment of incentives is the mechanism that turns a retainer into ownership. The strongest engagements pair a base retainer with a variable component tied to a metric the CRO genuinely controls — new bookings, qualified pipeline created, or net revenue retention — and sometimes a modest equity or advisory-share grant for longer commitments. Be wary of anyone who wants pure equity with no accountability, and equally wary of anyone who refuses any performance tie at all; both extremes signal misalignment. A confident operator will happily put a meaningful slice of their compensation at risk against results they believe they can deliver.

Finally, define the engagement's shape and exit up front. Fractional is often a bridge: to a full-time CRO hire later, to a specific fundraise or growth milestone, or to a turnaround of an underperforming team. Agree on the mandate, the 90-day plan, the metrics that define success, and the conditions under which the engagement scales up, winds down, or converts to a full-time search. A CRO who insists on an open-ended arrangement with no exit criteria may be optimizing for their own recurring revenue rather than your outcome. The [fractional engagement structuring guide](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/q11228) covers contract terms, notice periods, and conversion clauses in detail.

## What are the red flags that disqualify a fractional CRO

Some warning signs should end the conversation regardless of how polished the candidate is. The first is refusal to own a number — if they deflect accountability into "well, results depend on many factors," they are selling advice, not leadership. The second is a portfolio of too many concurrent clients: a fractional CRO juggling eight companies cannot possibly own your revenue with any depth. Ask how many active engagements they carry and how many hours total they've committed across all of them; if the math exceeds a reasonable work week, you will get the leftovers.

The third red flag is a title-heavy, outcome-light résumé — impressive company logos with no specific, verifiable revenue results attached. Fraud and inflation are common in the fractional market precisely because it is hard to verify. The fourth is discomfort with your actual stage or motion, papered over with confidence; a candidate who has only run enterprise field sales bluffing their way through a product-led-growth conversation will cost you a year. The fifth is any reluctance to provide direct references from the CEOs they reported to. Finally, watch for the leader who talks entirely about strategy and never about execution — in a lean Indiana company, the CRO must be willing to get in the CRM, sit on calls, and coach reps, not just philosophize in the boardroom.

## Related questions

### How much does a fractional CRO cost in Indiana?
Fees vary by hours and seniority, typically structured as a monthly retainer or day rate plus a performance or equity component. Focus on the commitment-to-price ratio and get weekly hours in writing rather than anchoring on a single dollar figure.

### Is a fractional CRO better than hiring full-time?
For companies under roughly $15–20M in revenue or those testing whether they need the role at all, fractional delivers senior expertise without the salary, equity, and hiring risk of a full-time CRO. Above that scale, or when the role needs daily presence, full-time usually wins.

### What is the difference between a fractional CRO and a sales consultant?
A fractional CRO owns the revenue number, runs the team, and is accountable for results; a consultant diagnoses and recommends while accountability stays with you. Look at whether their pay is tied to outcomes and whether they run your pipeline cadence.

### How many hours a week does a fractional CRO work?
Most commit one to three days — roughly 8 to 24 hours — depending on your stage and needs. Get the specific weekly commitment and the deliverables it maps to in writing before signing.

### Can a fractional CRO become full-time later?
Yes — many engagements are structured as a bridge to a full-time hire, and the fractional period doubles as an extended working interview. Define the conversion terms and timeline up front so both sides know the path.

## FAQ

**What should I look for first in a fractional CRO?**
Ownership of the number. Before regional fit, tech fluency, or fees, confirm they will actually carry and answer for the revenue result rather than merely advise on it. Everything else is secondary to that accountability.

**Does the CRO need to be physically located in Indiana?**
Not necessarily. Regional market fluency — understanding Midwest B2B buyers, Indiana's manufacturing and life-sciences base, and local talent costs — matters more than a Carmel address. A remote leader who knows your sector and stage often beats a local one who doesn't.

**How do I verify a fractional CRO's track record?**
Insist on specific, verifiable outcomes (starting and ending revenue, timeframe, their actual contribution) and speak directly with the CEOs they reported to. Ask those references whether they would hire the person again and how they handled a missed quarter.

**What stage company benefits most from a fractional CRO?**
Companies from roughly $1M to $20M in revenue that need senior revenue leadership but cannot justify or afford a full-time CRO. It also fits organizations testing whether they need the role, or navigating a specific transition like a fundraise or turnaround.

**Should a fractional CRO's pay be tied to performance?**
Ideally yes — a base retainer plus a variable component tied to a metric they control, such as bookings or net revenue retention, aligns their upside with yours. Be cautious of pure fixed retainers with no accountability and of pure equity deals with no base.

**How many clients should a fractional CRO have at once?**
Few enough that they can genuinely own your number — typically two to four active engagements. If the combined hours across all their clients exceed a reasonable work week, you will receive their leftover attention, not their ownership.

**What tech stack knowledge should a fractional CRO have?**
Deep fluency in your CRM (usually HubSpot or Salesforce), forecasting discipline, and the ability to build clean pipeline reporting. In a lean company they often serve as the RevOps function early on, so they must know what to build and what to defer.

**How long should a fractional CRO engagement last?**
Long enough to prove the motion and hit the 90-day plan, then reassessed against agreed success metrics. Many run six to twelve months as a bridge to a full-time hire, a fundraise, or a turnaround, with clear conditions for scaling up, winding down, or converting.
